answer.evidence: The main body is the pair of timber gates, drawn as a vertical face in rows 4-17 with planks, straps and rivets. Above them, rows 0-5 show only a thin grey railing rail and posts over the upper water. No plank walkway is drawn as a horizontal surface on top of the gates. Row 18 is a light line, but it sits below the gate face, so it reads as a sill beam rather than a top edge. Rows 19-24 are the sluice beam with vertical iron pipes and spouts, which also read as a vertical face. Rows 25 onward are foam and lower water, a flat water surface rather than part of the structure. No band, ellipse, roof or canopy shows a top surface for the gates, so the object reads as front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a canal lock, not a roofed building, but it is broadly comparable as a structure. Measured facts are close to the references: 12 visible tones per tile (references 12 and 10), 11% near-flat coverage (references 0%). The dark edge pixels are 58% near-neutral, against 7-9% for the references, so a good share of the outline is a neutral black/grey line, the sticker look. By eye, the timber gates have plank separation and a few iron strap highlights, but each material carries only about 4 steps, against 5-6 on the reference roofs and walls. The stone banks are repetitive blocks with light per-stone shading. The water and foam have some variation but are less rich than the reference tile scallops and plaster speckle. The neutral outlines and the shallower ramps keep it below the Beodeul bar.

answer.evidence: The main body is the pair of timber gates in rows 4-17. They are drawn as a flat vertical plank face with iron straps and rivets, and no front-edge line or eave shadow sits above them. Rows 0-3 hold only a thin rail and posts over water, about 2 rows of rim at most. Rows 18-24 hold a dark brown beam with a 1-row lighter line at row 18, vertical gray posts, and sluice spouts. That reads as a vertical beam face rather than a foreshortened walkway surface. Below it, rows 25-47 are water and foam. No horizontal plank walkway surface of 3 or more rows is clearly visible, so it reads as a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate's visible tones per tile (12) match the references (12 and 10), and near-flat coverage is 11% against 0% for both references. That puts it slightly more flat, though not badly so. The gate planks show about 3-4 brown steps with some grain, and the water has teal ramps with foam dots, so it is not a pure flat fill. 58% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, against 7-9% for the references. That reads as a partly near-black outline around the gate frame, the iron railing and the stone edges, which gives a more sticker-like look than the tinted material-tone outlines of Beodeul. The stone banks are small and sparse and lack the stone-by-stone shading of the stone reference. The plank deck and the capstans are simple. Overall it is competent but shallower than the references in ramp depth and outline craft. A careful artist would likely notice it looking flatter next to them.
